answers.answer: The API producer publishes the export job ID and inputs. It confirms the handoff through broker acceptance under its configured durability rules before returning accepted with the job ID. The broker holds the job until a worker receives it. The worker renders and saves the required downloadable file and ready status, then acknowledges processing so the broker can retire the delivery. Broker acceptance is not readiness: the saved required result permits ready status. Users need pending, ready and failed status, including a visible failed status if processing ultimately fails. A login decision must finish synchronously because access depends on that result; accepting a queued decision cannot justify granting access. One added operating cost is monitoring backlog and running workers.

evidence.quote: An API must confirm the handoff before telling the client the job was accepted.
Receives the message, saves the required result and ready status, then acknowledges processing to the broker.
Return a job ID and make pending, ready and failed status observable; ready means the required result has actually been saved.
Authorization must finish before granting access to a private resource; queueing that decision cannot justify granting access immediately.
The trade-off includes operating the broker and workers, tracking status, handling duplicates and retries, and watching backlog.

answers.answer: With at-least-once delivery the broker may redeliver the credited job because processing was not acknowledged. Acknowledging first could retire the delivery before a crash prevents the credit, losing work. Reuse the same stable business-operation ID on every retry. In a single database transaction insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table protected by a unique constraint and apply the balance credit: commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the credit. A separate lookup and credit is unsafe because concurrent attempts can race or a crash can split the steps. This makes that database effect duplicate-safe, not message delivery universally exactly once; it also does not atomically protect external effects.

evidence.quote: With at-least-once delivery, the broker can deliver the job again.
Acknowledging first instead risks losing the work if the worker crashes before saving it.
Reuse a stable business-operation ID across retries, not a new ID per attempt.
In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the job's database effect. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect.
It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

answers.answer: Retry the temporary image-store outage with increasing delays and a finite attempt or elapsed-time budget; avoid immediate repeated retries that deepen the outage. If the budget expires, move the job to a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status. Isolate the unsupported-format job directly, since waiting cannot fix its input, and expose failed status. Isolation lets healthy jobs continue. Before deliberately replaying either isolated job, fix its cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect; retain duplicate safety during replay. The lesson does not prescribe exact delay lengths or budget values.

evidence.quote: Retry with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget; immediate retries can deepen the outage.
An unsupported input format will not improve with waiting. Isolate it, or any job that exhausts its budget, in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status.
Healthy jobs can continue. Before deliberately replaying a failed job, fix its cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect. Replay still needs duplicate safety.

answers.answer: The later event can write 2 first, then the slower earlier event writes 5, leaving the wrong final quantity of 5. Receiving jobs in order does not force their effects to finish in order. Serialize effects for each item ID: the set-to-2 operation must wait while set-to-5 runs or retries. Different items may execute concurrently. If the first operation is dead-lettered, resolve whether to repair or cancel it before releasing its dependent update. A busy item becomes a throughput bottleneck because its dependent updates cannot execute in parallel.

evidence.quote: Delivery order and completion order are different.
Serialize effects per entity ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries. Different entities can still run in parallel. A busy entity becomes a throughput bottleneck.
Moving the earlier job to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates.

answers.answer: Backlog grows by about 120 - 80 = 40 jobs each second at those continuing rates. Increasing oldest-job age means the oldest unfinished work has waited longer and the promised client delay may be violated. Keep worker concurrency bounded at the image store safe limit rather than adding pressure to an already saturated dependency. Throttle or reject incoming requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer within an agreed limit, so accepted work can fit sustainable capacity. Queue storage and retention are finite; buffering only handles a burst if later capacity catches up before storage, retention or allowed-delay limits. More workers help when worker capacity is the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity, which the image store currently lacks.

evidence.quote: Watch backlog and oldest-job age: a growing wait can violate the promise to the client.
Storage and retention are finite. A queue can absorb a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached.
Bound worker concurrency to protect the database. Throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them within an agreed limit.
More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity.

answers.answer: One work queue distributes jobs among competing workers, so it does not independently give both billing and analytics every purchase; failed deliveries can nevertheless repeat. A retained log lets separate billing and analytics groups each read every purchase event independently, while workers inside each group share partitions. Each group tracks its own offset, or position, per partition. Recording progress by committing an offset does not delete the retained event. Analytics can rewind and replay the last day only if all required events for that day remain available under retention when replay is needed. A partition is an ordered slice, so ordering is per partition, not universal across partitions; adding partitions or consumers does not change that boundary. Retention and offsets do not make external effects exactly once. The lesson gives no mechanism by which adding consumers would atomically coordinate those effects.

evidence.quote: A work queue divides jobs among competing workers; it does not give every independent application every job. Failed deliveries can still repeat.
If billing and analytics each need every purchase event, separate consumer groups can track their own progress.
Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions. Committing an offset records progress; it does not delete the event.

A group can rewind and replay only while the required events remain under the retention policy. Ordering is per partition, not global. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.
